{{Short description|Signal processing technique}}
[[File:GPOF fit to noisy data.png|thumb|300px|Extraction of two sinusoids from a noisy data through the GPOF method]]
'''Generalized pencil-of-function method''' ('''GPOF'''), also known as '''matrix pencil method''', is a [[signal processing]] technique for estimating a signal or extracting information with [[Complex number|complex]] [[Exponential function|exponentials]]. Being similar to [[Prony method|Prony]] and original pencil-of-function methods, it is generally preferred to those for its robustness and computational efficiency.<ref name="matrix-pencil-1995"/>

The method was originally developed by Yingbo Hua and [[Tapan Kumar Sarkar|Tapan Sarkar]] for estimating the behaviour of electromagnetic systems by its transient response, building on Sarkar's past work on the original pencil-of-function method.<ref name="matrix-pencil-1995"/><ref name="suboptimal-1980"/> The method has a plethora of applications in [[electrical engineering]], particularly related to problems in [[computational electromagnetics]], [[microwave engineering]] and [[antenna (radio)|antenna theory]].<ref name="matrix-pencil-1995"/>

==Method==
===Mathematical basis===
A transient signal can be represented as:<ref name="generalized-1989"/>

:<math>y(t)=x(t)+n(t) \approx \sum_{i=1}^{M}R_i e^{s_i t} + n(t); 0 \leq t \leq T, </math>

where

: <math>y(t)</math> is the observed time-domain signal,
: <math>n(t)</math> is the [[Noise (signal processing)|signal noise]],
: <math>x(t)</math> is the actual signal,
: <math>R_i</math> are the [[Residue (complex analysis)|residues]] (<math>R_i</math>),
: <math>s_i</math> are the [[Zeros and poles|poles]] of the system, defined as <math>s_i=-\alpha_i+j \omega_i</math>,
: <math>z_i=e^{(- \alpha_i + j \omega_i) T_s}</math> by the identities of [[Z-transform]], 
: <math>\alpha_i</math> are the [[Damping ratio|damping factors]] and
: <math>\omega_i</math> are the [[angular frequency|angular frequencies]].

The same sequence, [[Sampling (signal processing)|sampled]] by a period of <math>T_s</math>, can be written as the following:

:<math>y[kT_s]=x[kT_s]+n[kT_s] \approx \sum_{i=1}^{M}R_i z_i^{k} + n[kT_s]; k=0,...,N-1; i=1,2,...,M</math>,

Generalized pencil-of-function estimates the optimal <math>M</math> and <math>z_i</math>'s.<ref name="hua-sarkar-1990"/>

===Noise-free analysis===
For the noiseless case, two <math>(N-L) \times L</math> matrices, <math>Y_1</math> and <math>Y_2</math>, are produced:<ref name="generalized-1989"/>

:<math>[Y_1]=
\begin{bmatrix}
x(0) & x(1) & \cdots & x(L-1)\\
x(1) & x(2) & \cdots & x(L)\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
x(N-L-1) & x(N-L) & \cdots & x(N-2)
\end{bmatrix}_{(N-L) \times L};
</math>{{fs}}<math>[Y_2]=
\begin{bmatrix}
x(1) & x(2) & \cdots & x(L)\\
x(2) & x(3) & \cdots & x(L+1)\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
x(N-L) & x(N-L+1) & \cdots & x(N-1)
\end{bmatrix}_{(N-L) \times L}
</math>

where <math>L</math> is defined as the [[Matrix pencil|pencil]] parameter. <math>Y_1</math> and <math>Y_2</math> can be decomposed into the following matrices:<ref name="generalized-1989"/>

:<math>[Y_1]=[Z_1][B][Z_2]</math>
:<math>[Y_2]=[Z_1][B][Z_0][Z_2]</math>

where

:<math>[Z_1]=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & \cdots & 1\\
z_1 & z_2 & \cdots & z_M\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
z_1^{(N-L-1)} & z_2^{(N-L-1)} & \cdots & z_M^{(N-L-1)}
\end{bmatrix}_{(N-L) \times M};
</math>{{fs}}<math>[Z_2]=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & z_1 & \cdots & z_1^{L-1}\\
1 & z_2 & \cdots & z_2^{L-1}\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
1 & z_M & \cdots & z_M^{L-1}
\end{bmatrix}_{M \times L}
</math>

<math display="inline">[Z_0]</math> and <math display="inline">[B]</math> are <math display="inline">M \times M</math> [[Diagonal matrix|diagonal matrices]] with sequentially-placed <math display="inline">z_i</math> and <math display="inline">R_i</math> values, respectively.<ref name="generalized-1989"/>

If <math display="inline">M \leq L \leq N-M</math>, the [[Generalized eigenvalue problem|generalized eigenvalues]] of the [[matrix pencil]]

:<math>[Y_2]-\lambda[Y_1]=[Z_1][B]([Z_0]-\lambda[I])[Z_2]</math>

yield the poles of the system, which are <math>\lambda=z_i</math>. Then, the generalized eigenvectors <math>p_i</math> can be obtained by the following identities:<ref name="generalized-1989"/>

:<math>[Y_1]^+[Y_1]p_i=p_i;</math>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<math>i=1,...,M</math>
:<math>[Y_1]^+[Y_2]p_i=z_i p_i;</math>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<math>i=1,...,M</math>

where the <math>^+</math> denotes the [[Moore–Penrose inverse]], also known as the pseudo-inverse. [[Singular value decomposition]] can be employed to compute the pseudo-inverse.

===Noise filtering===
If noise is present in the system, <math display="inline">[Y_1]</math> and <math display="inline">[Y_2]</math> are combined in a general data matrix, <math display="inline">[Y]</math>:<ref name="generalized-1989"/>

:<math>[Y]=
\begin{bmatrix}
y(0) & y(1) & \cdots & y(L)\\
y(1) & y(2) & \cdots & y(L+1)\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
y(N-L-1) & y(N-L) & \cdots & y(N-1)
\end{bmatrix}_{(N-L) \times (L+1)}
</math>

where <math>y</math> is the noisy data. For efficient [[Digital filter|filtering]], L is chosen between <math display="inline"> \frac{N}{3}</math> and <math display="inline"> \frac{N}{2}</math>. A singular value decomposition on <math display="inline">[Y]</math> yields:

:<math>[Y]=[U][\Sigma][V]^H</math>

In this decomposition, <math display="inline">[U]</math> and <math display="inline">[V]</math> are [[Unitary matrix|unitary matrices]] with respective [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvectors]] <math display="inline">[Y][Y]^H</math> and <math display="inline">[Y]^H[Y]</math> and <math display="inline">[\Sigma]</math> is a diagonal matrix with [[singular value]]s of <math display="inline">[Y]</math>. Superscript <math display="inline">H</math> denotes the [[conjugate transpose]].<ref name="generalized-1989"/><ref name="hua-sarkar-1990"/>

Then the parameter <math display="inline">M</math> is chosen for filtering. Singular values after <math display="inline">M</math>, which are below the filtering threshold, are set to zero; for an arbitrary singular value <math display="inline">\sigma_c</math>, the threshold is denoted by the following formula:<ref name="matrix-pencil-1995"/>

:<math>\frac{\sigma_c}{\sigma_{max}}=10^{-p}</math>,

<math display="inline">\sigma_{max}</math> and {{math|''p''}} are the maximum singular value and [[Significant figures|significant decimal digits]], respectively. For a data with significant digits accurate up to {{math|''p''}}, singular values below <math display="inline">10^{-p}</math> are considered noise.<ref name="hua-sarkar-1990"/>

<math display="inline">[V_1']</math> and <math display="inline">[V_2']</math> are obtained through removing the last and first row and column of the filtered matrix <math display="inline">[V']</math>, respectively; <math display="inline">M</math> columns of <math display="inline">[\Sigma]</math> represent  <math display="inline">[\Sigma']</math>. Filtered <math display="inline">[Y_1]</math> and <math display="inline">[Y_2]</math> matrices are obtained as:<ref name="hua-sarkar-1990"/>

:<math>[Y_1]=[U][\Sigma'][V_1']^H</math>
:<math>[Y_2]=[U][\Sigma'][V_2']^H</math>

Prefiltering can be used to combat noise and enhance [[signal-to-noise ratio]] (SNR).<ref name="matrix-pencil-1995"/> Band-pass matrix pencil (BPMP) method is a modification of the GPOF method via [[Finite impulse response|FIR]] or [[Infinite impulse response|IIR]] [[band-pass filter]]s.<ref name="matrix-pencil-1995"/><ref name="bpmp-paper"/>

GPOF can handle up to 25&nbsp;dB SNR. For GPOF, as well as for BPMP, variance of the estimates approximately reaches [[Cramér–Rao bound]].<ref name="generalized-1989"/><ref name="bpmp-paper"/><ref name="hua-sarkar-1990"/>

===Calculation of residues===
Residues of the complex poles are obtained through the [[least squares]] problem:<ref name="matrix-pencil-1995"/>

:<math>\begin{bmatrix}
y(0) \\ y(1) \\ \vdots \\ y(N-1)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\
z_1 & z_2 & \cdots & z_M \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 
z_1^{N-1} & z_2^{N-1} & \cdots & z_M^{N-1}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
R_1 \\ R_2 \\ \vdots \\ R_M
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

==Applications==
The method is generally used for the closed-form evaluation of Sommerfeld integrals in discrete complex image method for [[Method of moments (electromagnetics)|method of moments]] applications, where the spectral [[Green's function]] is approximated as a sum of complex exponentials.<ref name="matrix-pencil-1995"/><ref name="gpof-green"/> Additionally, the method is used in [[antenna (radio)|antenna]] analysis, [[Scattering parameters|S-parameter]]-estimation in [[Monolithic microwave integrated circuit|microwave integrated circuits]], wave propagation analysis, [[moving target indication]], [[Radar signal characteristics|radar signal processing]],<ref name="matrix-pencil-1995"/><ref name="kahrizi-slot"/><ref name="hua-radar"/> and [[series acceleration]] in electromagnetic problems.<ref name="summation-2016"/>
